title: Bowls
hookLine: the formal meal eaten from nested bowls, nothing wasted

lines: A BUNDLE TIED IN A CLOTH.
cards: A small bundle sits in front of each person in the hall: a cloth, tied with a neat knot. At the sound of a clapper, everyone unties it at the same moment.

Inside are bowls, one fitted inside the next like a set of measuring cups, plus a cloth, a spoon, chopsticks and a little spatula. The bowls come out in order and are set in a row. Servers walk the line with pots of food.
Nobody talks. Nobody reaches across. At the end, the bowls go back exactly as they came out, clean.

teach.h: A VESSEL THAT HOLDS JUST ENOUGH.
teach.b: First, the word. Oryoki is Japanese, often rendered as just enough: a vessel that holds exactly what is needed. You don't heap, and you don't leave a pile.
Second, one hand raised. When the server stops in front of you with a pot, you hold up a hand to signal enough. You take what you'll actually eat.
It's a tiny decision, made in silence with every serving, and it's the heart of the form: noticing, before the food lands, how much you really need. Third, the end of the meal.

teach.h: THE BOWLS RINSED, THE WATER DRUNK.
teach.b: Hot water is poured into the bowls. Each person cleans their bowl with the little spatula, moves the water to the next bowl and cleans that one too, then drinks the rinse water.
Tradition says a little of the water is set aside and offered to beings who go hungry. Not a grain of rice is left to throw away.
Fourth, no meal on autopilot. Before eating, the hall chants verses on how much work brought the food here, and on eating to sustain practice, not to indulge.
Oryoki takes something as automatic as eating and makes it impossible to do on autopilot.
On an ordinary workday, with a sandwich at a desk, the question it leaves is simple: how much is enough, and did I notice?

how: In many Zen monasteries and retreats, meals are eaten in the meditation hall in the oryoki style: participants unwrap a set of nested bowls, chant meal verses, receive food in silence, signal when they have enough, and clean their bowls with hot water at the end.

o: a Zen fast where the bowls are kept empty all day
a bell rung at the temple gate to call monks to eat
a formal Zen meal: take just what you need, waste nothing

p: rinses the bowls, then is drunk
offered to beings who go hungry

s: in oryoki, the server decides how much you get
you signal with a raised hand when there's enough.
after the bowls are cleaned, people drink it, so nothing is thrown away.
oryoki meals are a time for quiet conversation
the meal is eaten in silence, with set forms and chants.

games.q: you're at an oryoki meal. the server stops in front of you with a full pot, but you're not very hungry. what do you do?
o: take a full portion, to be polite.
raise a hand when there's just enough.
wave the server past and skip the food.
games.why: you signal when there's enough. the form isn't about refusing or overeating; it's about noticing what you'll actually eat, and eating all of it.

practice: Picture the next thing you'll eat, a meal or a snack, in front of you, and before it arrives, ask the oryoki question: how much is actually enough? Not what's polite, not what's on the plate.
Notice the answer and whether it surprises you, then picture the last bite and the empty bowl, clean, with nothing to throw away.

wordCard.voice: Oryoki. The formal Zen meal eaten from nested bowls: take just what you need, eat it with care, and leave nothing to waste. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: oryoki, the nested bowls and the meal, rendered 'just enough' or 'that which holds just enough'.

carryVoice: Your line: just enough. Not a grain left to throw away. Rest well.
